readerTitle: The new store layout 'won'. Do you roll it out?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (카페 카운터가 있는 차·간식 소매 체인) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: '이겼다'는 결과는 무엇과 비교했는지, 누구에게서 이겼는지, 어떤 지표로 이겼는지를 확인한 뒤에야 결정 근거가 된다.
misconception: 시범 매장 매출이 올랐으면 새 디자인이 효과가 있는 것이고, 평균이 오르면 모든 매장에 적용해도 된다.

sources.text: 통제 실험, 평균의 함정, 선행·후행 지표에 관한 표준 개념 (이 유닛의 앞선 레슨들)

factChecks.note: 1단계: 시범 매장 +14%, 나머지 8개 매장 +11%. 차이 3%p가 새 배치의 효과로 추정할 수 있는 최대치이며, 매장 선택이 무작위가 아니므로 이 값도 확실하지 않다는 점을 카드에 적었습니다.
2단계: 매장별 결과 +17%, +4%, −1%, 0%의 평균 = (17 + 4 − 1 + 0) ÷ 4 = 5%. 모두 같은 기간 대조 매장 대비 수치입니다.
3단계: 통근 매장에서 음료 판매 −8%, 진열대 판매 증가로 총매출은 대조 매장과 비슷(−1%, 0%). 모든 수치는 가상이며 서로 모순되지 않는지 다시 확인했습니다.

cards.title: The new store layout 'won'. Do you roll it out?
body: You run ten tea-and-snack shops, each with a small café counter. A designer moved the counter from the front to the back, so customers walk past the shelves to reach it.
Two shops tried it in November. Sales rose **14%** over October. The designer says: ship it to all ten.

image.label: A small shop with the café counter moved to the back
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 차·간식 가게의 위에서 본 단면도. 입구에서 안쪽 카페 카운터까지 진열대 사이로 점선 동선. 오른쪽 위에 "+14%" 말풍선. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sales are up 14%. What do you do first?
body: The designer picked the two pilot shops: your busiest, downtown. Rolling out costs about two weeks of work per shop.

options.text: Roll it out to all ten before the spring rush
options.feedback: You move fast, but November is gift season. If every shop rose anyway, you'd pay for ten refits based on the calendar, not the layout.

options.text: Check how the unchanged shops did in the same month
options.feedback: It costs one afternoon with the sales report. It tells you how much of the 14% would have happened without the change.

options.text: Ask customers in the pilot shops if they like the new layout
options.feedback: You learn something about the experience. But liking isn't buying, and you only hear from people who came in.

cards.title: The other shops rose too.
body: The eight unchanged shops grew **11%** in the same month. So the layout explains at most about 3 points, not 14.
Even that is shaky. The pilot shops were hand-picked busy stores, so they may simply have had a better month.

image.label: The other shops rose too.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: A fair test says +5%. Ship it now?
body: Say you ran a proper test. Four shops, picked at random, got the new layout. Four similar shops stayed the same. After six weeks, the new-layout shops beat the others by **5%** on average.

options.text: Yes. A fair test with a clear average gain is enough
options.feedback: The test was fair, but one average can hide very different shops. You might refit stores where the layout hurts.

options.text: Look at each of the four shops before deciding
options.feedback: Ten minutes of work. You find out whether the gain is everywhere or in one place.

options.text: Keep testing for six more months to be sure
options.feedback: More data helps, but it delays any gain and keeps four shops half-decided. Look closer at what you already have first.

cards.title: One shop carried the average.
body: The 5% came almost entirely from the shop near the university. Students browse, and the snack wall now sits at the door. In commuter shops, people want a quick drink. Walking to the back slowed them down.

breakdown.label: Shop A
breakdown.detail: Near a university, lots of browsing

cards.softwareNote: An app A/B test can fool you the same way. A 5% lift in sign-ups may come entirely from new visitors, while long-time users quietly use the product less.

cards.title: The commuter shops look flat. Is flat safe?
body: In shops C and D, café drink sales fell **8%**. Extra snack sales roughly made up for it, so total sales look flat. Many drink buyers are morning regulars who come in four or five times a week.

options.text: Roll out everywhere. Flat totals mean no harm
options.feedback: Totals are flat today, but fewer regular visits now usually mean lower sales later. You'd find out in the yearly numbers, too late to undo cheaply.

options.text: Use the layout in browsing shops only, and track regulars' weekly visits
options.feedback: You keep the clear win where it works and protect your most loyal customers. Watching visits warns you before sales fall.
Safe for regulars, but you give up a 17% gain in shops where browsing is the whole point.

cards.title: Fair tests have limits too.
body: With four shops on each side, a local road closure or a new competitor can swing a result by several points. Treat small differences as a hint, not proof.
Six weeks also catches novelty. A new layout can lift sales simply because it's new.
And testing costs time. For cheap changes you can easily undo, like a new shelf sign, just try it and watch.

image.label: Small test groups with one store swayed by a local event
image.brief: 가게 아이콘 8개를 두 줄(새 배치 4, 기존 배치 4)로 배치. 그중 한 가게 옆에만 "Road works" 공사 표지판과 흔들리는 막대 그래프. 차분한 톤의 인포그래픽, 로고 없음.

cards.title: A win only counts once you know: compared to what, for whom, and measured how.
body: Each decision used one idea from this unit.
list: **Decision 1:** compare against shops that didn't change, and don't let anyone hand-pick the test stores. *Controlled experiments, selection bias*
**Decision 2:** split the average before you trust it. *Averages hide the story*
**Decision 3:** watch what predicts future sales, not just today's total. *Leading vs lagging indicators*
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick the last change you called a success. Write down what you compared it to and which customers it helped.
